extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and applicants (Korean Patent Office guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidance for assessing whether a claimed invention involves an inventive step (obviousness) when examining patent applications, including definitions, prior-art selection, procedural steps, motivation/obviousness factors, and consideration of advantageous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art, the invention does not have an inventive step (Article 29(2) of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is not defined in the Act, but the guideline states that an invention that 'could have been easily made' by a skilled person lacks inventive step. The examiner must decide whether the claimed invention could have been easily made alone or by combining prior art references; if so, inventive step is denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior to filing of a patent application (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Prior to filing of a patent application” refers not simply to the filing date but to the definite time (hours and minutes) of filing of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When foreign disclosures precede the Korean filing time (local time), they are considered prior art under Article 29(1). Precise filing time matters for determining whether a disclosure is prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person who has common general knowledge in the relevant art, can use ordinary technical means for R&D (experiments, analysis, manufacture), can exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials and changing designs, and can comprehend the state of the art at the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described as an expert able to comprehend all technical matters relevant to the problem to be solved by the claimed invention. This characterisation guides what a skilled person would find obvious or be motivated to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art (what it includes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art at filing includes inventions in Article 29(1) subparagraphs, common general knowledge, and other publicly known technical matters, including ordinary methods to conduct daily work and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider all types of information relevant to the technical field of the invention described in the claims when assessing novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention that could have been easily made (interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person skilled in the art could have easily conceived the claimed invention by exercising ordinary creativity or motivated by prior-disclosed inventions prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concept underpins the inventive-step inquiry and is used to judge if differences from prior art are merely routine or expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles of determining inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art from prior art references (alone or combined). If so, the invention lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the determination to each claim separately; novelty determination should come first (distinct from inventive-step determination). Examiners may notify applicants of novelty and inventive-step grounds together, but the analyses are distinct. For claims with multiple inventions/Markush groups, the examiner must precisely point out which invention is rejected and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's holistic method of determining inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider the overall state of the art a skilled person would consider at filing, and thoroughly consider the invention's purpose, technical configuration, advantageous effects, and applicant arguments, focusing on the difficulty of the claimed technical configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination should comprehensively weigh purpose/effectiveness and focus on whether the claimed configuration would have been difficult to arrive at for a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key focal points in inventive-step assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should consider whether (1) prior art provides motivation to arrive at the claimed invention, or (2) differences are a mere exercise of ordinary creativity, and (3) whether the claimed invention has advantageous effects over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three considerations are to be balanced when assessing whether the claimed invention involves an inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for determining inventive step (stepwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Specify the claimed invention; 2) Specify scope/content of prior art references from the viewpoint of a skilled person; 3) Choose the closest prior art and compare as a whole; 4) Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made in view of prior art or common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying claimed invention and prior art scope uses the same methods as novelty determination. The combined elements of an invention should be compared as a whole (not separated) to corresponding elements in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of prior art reference (relevant technical field)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a principle, the prior art used for comparison should be selected from the same technical field or a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'same technical field' usually refers to the industrial field of application but can also be inferred from effects/functions of claim elements. A prior art from a different field can be used if it might be applied across fields or would be used by an applicant in solving the technical problem; examiner should consider relevance, closeness of problems, and similarity of function/work/operation. Examples (container cap vs. eruption closure; umbrella vs. parasol) illustrate relevance-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the closest prior art reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The most relevant prior art that a person skilled in the art would choose and which discloses most of the technical features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desirable to pick the closest reference from inventions in proximate technical fields or those having the same effect/use/problem. Examples: umbrella as closest prior art for parasol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of prior art that teaches away
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art contains a description that teaches away from the claimed technical idea, examiners should be careful selecting it as a prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a prior art teaches away, it can still be relied upon if other aspects (close relation of technical fields, similarity of function, etc.) make it possible to arrive at the claimed invention (e.g., by combining features from multiple references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of applicant's admission of background art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant admits that background art in the specification was publicly known prior to filing, novelty can be assessed on that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special circumstances (e.g., earlier application not published, internal company knowledge not public) can reverse the assumption if the applicant proves or asserts such cases; then a ground for rejection based on the assumption may be remedied and examination continued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incomplete or imperfect prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art reference is an incomplete invention (insufficient disclosure), it can still be cited in determining inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a skilled person can recognize relevant facts or effects from the incomplete disclosure and they are not contrary to technical common sense at filing, the reference may be used (example: pharmaceutical effects inferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause or motivation (grounds for obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong grounds that a skilled person would have been led to the claimed invention include suggestions in prior-disclosed references, close similarity of the problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, or close relevance of technical fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors indicate motivation to combine or adapt prior art to reach the claimed invention; they are enumerated and illustrated with examples in the guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions in prior art disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions shown in the disclosures of prior art references relevant to the claimed invention can be strong grounds that a skilled person would be led to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art implicitly or explicitly suggests components or configurations that bring the claimed feature within routine design choices, the claimed feature may be deemed obvious (example: heat exchanger implicitly suggested in cooling apparatus reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of the problem to be solved
rubrics_metrics.description: If the technical problems of the claimed invention and prior art are closely similar, this can be strong ground that a skilled person would arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners decide whether problems correspond and whether reasoning from prior art makes the claimed invention obvious. Even when problems differ, if a skilled person can arrive at the claimed invention without creative thinking, inventive step can be denied (examples: combining animal-shaped cap and face-protecting hood; applying thermally-actuated methods to pressure-actuated diaphragms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of function, work, or operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A close similarity in function, work, or operation between claimed invention and prior art (or between prior art references) supports a finding that a skilled person would arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If functions/operations match, applying a component from one reference to another may be obvious (example: transferring a filtering part structure from automobile filter to home filter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Close relation of technical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly known technical means from a related technical field can be a strong ground that a skilled person could easily make the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fields are related (e.g., gloves vs socks), techniques from one may be applied to the other as routine adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common improvements based on general application of prior art, reasoning based on known physical properties, or referring to other fields to solve a known problem are ordinary creativity and do not indicate inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of ordinary creativity include selecting optimal known materials, optimizing numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, simple design modifications, partial removal of features, and simple change/limitation of use. If differences fall only into these categories without unexpected advantages, inventive step is usually negated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement with equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing an element with a publicly known compatible means having the same function is not inventive if it does not exhibit an unexpected advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To treat such substitution as ordinary creativity, it must be obvious to a skilled person at filing that the substitute is an equivalent; examiner may submit evidence that substitution was known as equivalent. Examples include substituting SiC with aluminum when equivalence was known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple modification of design in applying a known technology
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention is arrived at by a mere simple modification of design without changing the prior art's technical idea and yields no advantageous effect, inventive step cannot be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences only in parameters (size, proportion, dimensions, amounts) from limited ranges are typically obvious unless they produce unexpected functional changes. Examples: modification of microwave door protrusions; altering microcomputer resistance values for another appliance—may be routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial removal of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of some features readily mentioned in prior art that removes related function/effect and is obvious to a skilled person is not inventive, unless omission does not affect function or unexpectedly enhances it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: removing a protective silicate from toothpaste to lower cost, which also removes the protective effect—such omission is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple change or limitation of use
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention that merely uses a known invention in a further simple restricted way, without showing any advantageous effect, is not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reusing a synthetic oil as cutting oil when recycling would be naturally expected—such mere change of use negates inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: General application of known art
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique in a closely analogous situation to solve a prior-art problem with readily anticipated effect is not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if application yields unexpected beneficial effects in combination with other components, inventive step may be acknowledged. Examples: transforming a conventional medicine into liquid form may be routine; forming a leak-detecting hole may be common practice; adopting ball grid arrays when trend already prevalent is routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of advantageous effects to support inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If matters defining a claimed invention achieve effects advantageous over prior art, those effects are considered to support inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarkable advantageous effects not foreseeable by a skilled person from the state of the art can justify granting inventive step even if combination seems straightforward. Particularly important for selection inventions and chemical inventions where effects are hard to predict. Examiner may consider applicant's arguments and experimental evidence only if effects are inferable from description/drawings or supported by evidence; unsupported assertions should not be considered. Case law references (Supreme Court decisions) illustrate when effects can overcome obviousness.
